content: Treatment is generally advised for patients with an average risk of Clostridium difficile (C. difficile) infection who exhibit symptoms and have positive laboratory results. For patients with risk factors for C. difficile, empiric therapy is recommended even if laboratory findings are negative, provided they are symptomatic. The choice of antimicrobial therapy is determined by the clinical severity of the infection. Oral metronidazole is the preferred treatment for patients with mild symptoms, while oral vancomycin is recommended for those with severe disease. Treatment is only indicated for symptomatic individuals with positive laboratory findings for C. difficile infection, such as diarrhea confirmed by ELISA or PCR testing. Asymptomatic individuals or those with diarrhea but negative laboratory results do not require treatment. For patients with an average risk of developing C. difficile infection, the negative predictive value of diagnostic tests like ELISA or PCR is high (greater than 95%). Therefore, empiric therapy is not recommended for these patients if laboratory results are negative. However, for high-risk patients, the negative predictive value of these tests is insufficient. As a result, empiric therapy is recommended for high-risk individuals with a high pre-test probability of infection, even if laboratory findings are negative. Common risk factors for C. The 2013 guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of C. difficile infection recommend tailoring antimicrobial therapy based on the severity of the disease. Antimicrobial therapy should be administered for 10 to 14 days, but if clinical improvement is observed within 5 to 7 days, the therapy can be limited to 10 days. During treatment, other antibiotic therapies should be suspended. Vancomycin is recommended for mild-to-moderate cases in patients who are intolerant or allergic to metronidazole, as well as for pregnant or breastfeeding women. Supportive care should be provided for patients with severe or complicated C. difficile infection. For patients with worsening diarrhea or abdominal pain, an abdominal CT scan should be performed to rule out complications. Surgical consultation and pre-surgical work-up are necessary for patients suspected of having complicated C. difficile infection. Fecal microbiota transplantation should be considered for patients with a third recurrence after a pulsed vancomycin regimen. A vancomycin enema may be used for patients whose oral antibiotic regimen cannot reach certain segments of the colon, such as those with Hartman’s pouch, ileostomy, or colon diversion. Intravenous immunoglobulins should only be administered for recurrent C. difficile infection in patients with hypogammaglobulinemia. For patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and concurrent C. difficile infection, the infection should be managed alongside the IBD flare-up, and immunosuppressive medications should be continued. Metronidazole should not be used for a second recurrence of C. difficile infection or for long-term therapy due to the risk of neurotoxicity. Anti-peristaltic agents should not be used to treat diarrhea in patients with C. difficile infection. Intravenous immunoglobulins should not be administered for recurrent C. difficile infection unless the patient has hypogammaglobulinemia. Immunosuppressive medications should not be increased in IBD patients with untreated C. difficile infection. Fidaxomicin, a poorly absorbed, bactericidal, macrocyclic antibiotic targeting anaerobic, gram-positive bacteria, was approved by the FDA in 2011 for the treatment of C. difficile infection. It has been shown to be non-inferior to vancomycin for treating primary infections. Fidaxomicin is associated with a significantly lower recurrence rate compared to vancomycin (15% vs. 25%), except in cases involving the BI/NAP1/027 strain, where recurrence rates are similar between the two therapies. Fecal bacteriotherapy, also known as fecal microbiota transplantation, is a procedure that involves the infusion of bacterial flora from the feces of a healthy donor. This approach aims to restore the bacterial balance in the gut and has been suggested as a potential cure for recurrent C. difficile infection.
